source_text: Quin potius memores simus tam dominicarum pronuntiationum quam apostolicarum litterarum, quae nobis et futuras haereses praenuntiaverunt et fugiendas praefinierunt, et sicut esse illas non expavescimus, ita et posse id, propter quod effugiendae sunt, non miremur. Instruit dominus multos esse venturos sub pellibus ovium rapaces lupos. Quaenam istae sunt pelles ovium, nisi nominis Christiani extrinsecus superficies? Qui lupi rapaces, nisi sensus et spiritus subdoli, ad infestandum gregem Christi intrinsecus delitescentes? Qui pseudoprophetae sunt, nisi falsi praedicatores? Qui pseudoapostoli, nisi adulteri evangelizatores? Qui antichristi interim et semper, nisi Christi rebelles? Hoc erunt haereses non minus doctrinarum perversitate ecclesiam lacessentes quam tunc antichristus persecutionem atrocitate persequetur; nisi quod persecutio et martyras facit, haeresis apostatas tantum. Et ideo haereses quoque oportebat esse, ut probabiles quique manifestarentur, tam qui in persecutionibus steterint quam qui ad haereses non exorbitaverint. Neque enim eos probabiles intellegi iuvat qui in haeresin fidem demutant; sicut ex diverso sibi interpretantur, quia dixerit alibi, Omnia examinate, quod bonum est tenete. Quasi non liceat omnibus male examinatis in electionem alicuius mali impingere per errorem.
thought_title: Heresies were foretold and serve to test the faithful
orientation: Tertullian is addressing believers, urging them to remember that the Lord and the apostles predicted heresies and commanded them to be avoided, so their existence should not cause alarm.
pass_a_gloss: Rather let us be mindful both of the Lord's pronouncements and of the apostolic letters, which both announced to us that heresies would come in the future and prescribed that they must be fled, and just as we do not fear that they exist, so also let us not be surprised that that can happen on account of which they must be fled. The Lord teaches that many will come under the skins of sheep as ravenous wolves. What are these skins of sheep, except the outward surface of the Christian name? What ravenous wolves, except deceitful thoughts and spirits, hiding within to attack the flock of Christ? What are false prophets, except false preachers? What false apostles, except adulterous evangelizers? What antichrists, both for now and always, except rebels against Christ? These will be the heresies, attacking the church no less by the perversity of their doctrines than the antichrist will then pursue it by the cruelty of persecution; except that persecution also makes martyrs, heresy only apostates. And therefore heresies also had to exist, so that whoever are approved might be made manifest, both those who have stood firm in persecutions and those who have not swerved toward heresies. For it does not help that those be understood as approved who change their faith into heresy; just as they interpret for themselves from the opposite direction, because he said elsewhere, Examine all things, hold what is good. As if it were not permitted for all who have examined badly to stumble into the choice of some evil through error.

choices.english: under the skins of sheep as ravenous wolves
choices.why: Keeps the literal image of wolves wearing sheep skins, matching the Gospel wording and Tertullian's rhetorical question that follows.
rejected: in sheep's clothing as ravenous wolves

choices.why: Preserves the strong moral charge of 'adulteri' as corrupters of the gospel message, not merely false teachers.

choices.english: whoever are approved might be made manifest
choices.why: Keeps the passive force of 'probabiles' (those who are approved/tested) and the purpose clause, matching the testing function of heresies.
rejected: those who are genuine might be shown

choices.why: Literal rendering of the accusative of direction, showing the transformation of faith into heresy.

choices.term: Omnia examinate, quod bonum est tenete
choices.english: Examine all things, hold what is good
choices.why: Direct rendering of the Pauline command, preserving the imperative force and the contrast between examining and holding.
rejected: Test everything, hold fast what is good

Omnia examinate, quod bonum est tenete

pass_b_english: Let us rather remember both the Lord's pronouncements and the apostolic letters, which announced to us beforehand that heresies would come and prescribed beforehand that they must be avoided. Just as we are not terrified that they exist, so let us not be surprised that they can do the very thing for which they must be avoided.

The Lord teaches that many will come under the skins of sheep as ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). What are those sheep skins but the outward surface of the Christian name? What are the ravenous wolves but deceitful minds and spirits, hiding within to attack the flock of Christ? What are the false prophets but false preachers? What are the false apostles but adulterous evangelizers? What are the antichrists, now and always, but rebels against Christ? These are the heresies, attacking the church with the perversity of their doctrines no less than the antichrist will then pursue it with the cruelty of persecution. The difference is this: persecution makes martyrs, while heresy makes only apostates.

And therefore heresies also had to exist, so that whoever are approved might be made manifest, both those who have stood firm in persecutions and those who have not swerved aside into heresies. For it does not avail to understand as approved those who change their faith into heresy. Yet the heretics interpret it otherwise for themselves, because Paul said elsewhere, Examine all things, hold what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). As if it were not permitted for those who have examined badly to stumble into the choice of some evil through error.

problems.quote: For it does not please him that those who change their faith into heresy should be understood as approved.
problems.source_quote: Neque enim eos probabiles intellegi iuvat qui in haeresin fidem demutant
problems.why: 'iuvat' means 'it helps/avails', not 'it pleases him'; no subject 'him' in source. The sense is: it does not help to understand as approved those who change faith into heresy.
problems.fix: For it does not avail to understand as approved those who change their faith into heresy.
problems.ruling: Latin 'iuvat' is impersonal ('it helps/pleases'), no explicit 'him'; translation adds 'him' and shifts meaning

edits.old: For it does not please him that those who change their faith into heresy should be understood as approved.
edits.new: For it does not avail to understand as approved those who change their faith into heresy.

fixed: Corrected 'does not please him' to 'does not avail' because 'iuvat' means 'it helps/avails', not 'it pleases him'; no subject 'him' in source.

problems.quote: as if it were not possible, after examining everything badly, to stumble into the choice of some evil through error.
problems.source_quote: Quasi non liceat omnibus male examinatis in electionem alicuius mali impingere per errorem.
problems.why: Latin says ‘it is not permitted’, not ‘it is not possible’; modality is changed.
problems.fix: as if it were not permitted for those who have examined badly to be led into the choice of some evil by error.
problems.ruling: Latin 'non liceat' = 'not permitted'; English 'not possible' changes modality from permission to capability.

edits.old: as if it were not possible, after examining everything badly, to stumble into the choice of some evil through error.
edits.new: as if it were not permitted for those who have examined badly to stumble into the choice of some evil through error.

fixed: Changed 'possible' to 'permitted' to match 'liceat' (it is permitted), and adjusted the construction to reflect 'omnibus male examinatis' (those who have examined badly).

problems.quote: Yet they interpret it otherwise for themselves, because he said elsewhere, Examine all things, hold what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
problems.why: 'He' is Paul but antecedent is unclear after the previous paragraph's discussion of Christ's words.

edits.old: Yet they interpret it otherwise for themselves, because he said elsewhere, Examine all things, hold what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
edits.new: Yet they interpret it otherwise for themselves, because Paul said elsewhere, Examine all things, hold what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21)

fixed: The source says 'quia dixerit alibi' — 'because he said elsewhere.' The 'he' refers to Paul, whose letters were just mentioned at the start of the passage ('apostolicarum litterarum'). The English 'he' is ambiguous after the intervening discussion of Christ's words, so specifying 'Paul' is a legitimate clarification that fits the source.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker of the final Scripture quotation as Paul, named the heretics as the ones interpreting it, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and reference.
